results.content:
The fix is usually a split rather than a migration. Keep Confluence as the internal wiki, where the Jira links and co-editing earn their keep, and publish the customer-facing subset of your documentation in a tool built for publishing. Your Confluence instance is untouched by this, so it isn’t a bet, and you can run both for as long as you like.

The honest cost is two tools and two bills. What you get back is an internal wiki that stays useful to engineers and a help center that’s somebody’s entire product rather than a share setting. If you’re not sure where the line falls, internal vs external knowledge base is ten minutes well spent before you book any demos.

## Moving your documentation off Confluence [...] If the wiki is the problem, replace it with a better wiki. Slite if you want the same job done cleanly with AI that flags drift, Notion if the content is free-form team docs and you’d like one workspace for everything, Bloomfire if the real issue is that knowledge is scattered across a dozen systems at company scale and you have enterprise budget to fix it.

If your documentation is formal rather than collaborative, go to a documentation platform. GitBook when engineers own the docs and Git is the natural home, Document360 the moment versioning, approvals, or auditors enter the conversation. [...] Best for teams who need a customer-facing knowledge base, not a wiki. Flat $129/mo, public readers free. Start a free trial or see pricing.

## Best for company-wide internal knowledge: Bloomfire

If your real Confluence problem is that knowledge is scattered across five systems and nobody can find any of it, Bloomfire aims directly at that. It indexes 25+ file types and automatically transcribes video and audio, so a phrase somebody said in a recorded all-hands becomes searchable text you can jump straight to. Its connectors make SharePoint, Google Drive, Salesforce, Teams, and Confluence itself searchable from one place, so it can sit on top of the mess rather than asking you to clean it up first.

If you want to explore what a modern knowledge base can feel like without the plugin overload, ONES Wiki gives you a robust foundation that mimics the best Confluence patterns but removes the headaches.

## Common Challenges When Scaling a Confluence Knowledge Base

Even with great examples, you’ll hit roadblocks as your wiki grows. Here are the most common issues—and how to fix them.

### Challenge: Content sprawl makes navigation a nightmare

After a year, you have 500 pages and no clear folder logic. Solution: run a quarterly “tree audit.” Drag pages into a temporary review space and only move back what still serves a purpose. Archive the rest with a clear “archived” label so it doesn’t pollute search results.

### Challenge: New team members ignore the wiki and ask in chat [...] This is a cultural problem. Fix it by creating a rule: if someone asks a question that has a wiki page, the answer must be a link, never a direct text response. The wiki becomes the single source of truth gradually.

### Challenge: Outdated content erodes trust

Place a “last verified” date macro on every page and set a Confluence automation to notify the owner when a page goes stale. If you use ONES Wiki, the built‑in page analytics can automatically surface unvisited pages to flag them for a refresh.

### Challenge: Merging knowledge bases after a company acquisition [...] Modern alternatives like ONES Wiki, Notion, and GitBook all offer streamlined knowledge base features with less reliance on plugins. ONES Wiki stands out because it provides on‑premise deployment and native analytics without add‑ons, making it a strong Confluence alternative for teams that want simplicity and full control. The right choice depends on your requirements for security, collaboration, and budget.
